content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed a novel method of Meta-Surrogate Model (MSM) which can generate more transferable adversarial examples in the black-box adversarial attacks. The problem is formulated as a bi-level-like optimization problem which achieved via a differentiable attacker. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in generating the transferable adversarial examples.
content.main_review:
In general, the paper is clearly written and easy to follow but I still have several concerns:
1.	The authors are expected to clarify their technical contributions, or what are the main advantages of the Meta-Surrogate Model compared with the ensemble-based adversarial attacks. 
2.	The authors are expected to make more comprehensive analysis on the computational cost of the algorithms especially when the number of the source models are increasing. Is it fair to compare the performance with the alternative methods since the authors actually use multiple source models and more gradient information? 
3.	The authors are expected to demonstrate the transferability especially when the network structures are significantly, e.g., the vision transformers. 
4.	In some cases, one may expect a better transferability by averaging or smoothing the gradient such as the DIM or TI-based methods. I think the proposed method in this paper is actually averaging the gradient on the source models which is similar the to previous works.

display_title: Response to question: The proposed method in this paper is actually averaging the gradient on the source models?

content.title: Response to question: The proposed method in this paper is actually averaging the gradient on the source models?
content.comment:
The proposed MTA does not average the gradient of source models.
Figure 7 can prove our viewpoint.
Figure 7 shows the adversarial examples and the corresponding noise maps generated by MTA and baselines when the source model is ResNet-152.
It is clear that when using a single source model ResNet-152, the adversarial noise maps generated by MTA differ greatly from those generated by baselines.
**It seems that MTA learns some specific noise patterns to improve transfer attack but does not try to directly average or smooth the gradient from the source model.
Moreover, the adversarial noise maps generated by MTA contain clearer semantic information than baselines, which may explain why MTA is more effective than baselines to generate transferable adversarial examples.**

Overall, **the proposed MTA outperforms the baselines** and the improvement comes from the proposed bi-level optimization framework.
MTA does not try to average or smooth the gradient from the source models.

We hope that our response has addressed your concerns, and turns your assessment to the positive side. If you have other comments, we are glad to address them.

display_title: Response to question: The proposed MTA actually use multiple source models and more gradient information?

content.title: Response to question: The proposed MTA actually use multiple source models and more gradient information?
content.comment:
**The comparison between the proposed MTA and the baselines is fair.**
In each testing scene, the available source models are consistent for MTA and baselines.
For example, when doing experiments on Cifar-10, we use the eight source models to implement all baselines, and we still use the same eight source models to implement MTA.
Compared with baselines, we did not use any additional source models to improve MTA.
**The key difference between the PGD-based baselines and MTA is that the baselines directly use the source models to generate transferable adversarial examples while MTA does not directly use the source models to generate adversarial examples.
MTA firstly uses the source models to obtain a meta-surrogate model and then uses the single meta-surrogate model to generate transferable adversarial examples.**

Besides, MTA does not use more gradient information than baselines.
The number of gradient ascent steps is set equally for MTA and baselines.
**The advantage of MTA is that the gradient direction attacking the meta-surrogate model is more effective than the gradient direction attacking the source models to be transferred to attack target models.**
Overall, the comparison between MTA and the baselines is fair.

content.comment:
Thanks for your question.
We have analyzed the computational cost in Section A.8 (Section A.10 in the revision version).
The training cost of the proposed MTA depends mainly on the backbone of MSM, the used source models, the dataset, the batch size, $T_t$, and etc.
As Eq.6 shows, each source model is denoted as $\mathcal{F}_i$ and there will be more $\mathcal{F}_i$ when the number of source models $N$ is increasing.
 Clearly, the larger the number of source models $N$, the more computational cost to compute the gradient in Eq.6.

display_title: Response to question: The authors are expected to clarify their technical contributions, what are the main advantages of the Meta-Surrogate Model compared with the ensemble-based adversarial attacks.

content.title: Response to question: The authors are expected to clarify their technical contributions, what are the main advantages of the Meta-Surrogate Model compared with the ensemble-based adversarial attacks.
content.comment:
The technical contributions of our work can be summarized as follows:  
1. We propose a novel viewpoint that directly attacking the source models is not the most suitable way to generate transferable adversarial examples, and there should exist more suitable surrogate models than source models for transfer attack.
2. To verify our viewpoint, we develop a novel framework called meta-transfer attack (MTA) which trains a particular surrogate model (meta-surrogate model) for transfer attack.
Besides, to enable the gradient back-propagating in all the MTA framework, we design a novel Customized-PGD for MTA.
3. Extensive experiments on Cifar-10 and ImageNet demonstrate that there do exist meta-surrogate models that are more suitable than source models to address the transfer attack problem. 
The experiments also demonstrate the importance of the proposed Customized PGD for MTA.

**The advantage of the meta-surrogate model is that attacking it is an easier way than attacking the ensemble-based source models to generate transferable adversarial examples.**

content.summary_of_the_paper: A complete black box adversarial attack thus far has not performed well as research shows. By complete black box, it means there is no information available about the target model, not even query based probing. Most SOTA uses a surrogate model to generate adversarial examples, where the surrogate model may, every likely, not in any way resemble the target model in practice. This paper claims that by adopting a meta training scheme, more effective black box attacks are achievable when compared to the SOTA.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- As far as I know, the proposed meta training scheme is novel.
- Writing is decent, but i think it can be simplified a bit more or some parts explain a bit better. More in "weaknesses".
- I also appreciate that the authors provide larger dataset results, aka on imagenet, which is quite expensive to run for adversarial attack work.

Weaknesses:
- First off, iiuc, the MSM is trained by assuming that the dataset used by the target model is known (mentioned in first paragraph under "Methodology"). If this paper's prime motivation is that it is a truly black box attack, I find this assumption compromising. In practice, for black box attack, the dataset used by the target model is likely unknown, and in many cases, updated continuously.
- On page 4, it says "Section 3.3 will show more explanations ..." which I don't find that to be the case. Section 3.3 in fact assume Eq. 4. Did I misunderstand the writing?
- Can we properly define success rate in experiments? Even if it is well defined in literature or it is straightforward, I think we should define what it is.
- Can we provide clarity how is MTA and IR combine? Unless I missed it, this was quickly gleaned over in one sentence. It helps me to understand the impact of IR In MTA.
- The empirical results are ok but some concerns remain for me. On imagenet, MTA and its variants are not always the best performing, sometimes by a somewhat significant margin. Also, it is quite befuddling that the single source model results seem to be better than multiple source models, which is a bit counter-intuitive.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I felt the paper has merits as the idea of meta learning to achieve generalized AE may be novel. Unless, I did not understand the paper fully, the design choices in Eq. 4 may be explained more clearly -- intuitively I can see why they help but a more formal ex-position may make the paper better. 

My biggest issue is that the paper assume that the dataset used by the target model is known. This takes away a lot of the wow factor for me as I definitely appreciate how difficult it is to achieve real-world black box adversarial attacks. This paper could have been better it experiments have been conducted in the case where the target model's dataset is unknown or even continuously updating.

The next issue I have is that MTA and its variants do not always show to be the overwhelming winner in the benchmarks, especially on the imagenet results. I think that is ok, as I do appreciate the difficulty running adversarial attacks on imagenet but more insights on why will make the paper better.

If these concerns can be somewhat mitigated this time round, I will change my rating. However, even if not, this paper is still a good paper for the next conference once things are further beefed up.

display_title: Response to question: MTA and its variants do not always show to be the overwhelming winner in the benchmarks, especially on the imagenet results.

content.title: Response to question: MTA and its variants do not always show to be the overwhelming winner in the benchmarks, especially on the imagenet results.
content.comment:
Thanks for you advice.
In our viewpoint, the possible reason why MTA cannot perform the best on all benchmarks is that **the architecture of MSM may be unsuitable in some benchmarks.**
For example, as Table 2 shows, MTA performs not always the best when using the IncRes-V2 source model.
In our experiment, we found that training the MSM with ResNet-19 backbone to attack the IncRes-V2 source model is more difficult to converge than training the MSM to attack other source models.
We guess the possible reason for this phenomenon is that the gradient information of ResNet-19 differs greatly from that of IncRes-V2, and IncRes-V2 is not easy to lead ResNet-19 to adjust its weight to ensure the adversarial attack on it can also fool IncRes-V2.
In other words, the feedback information IncRes-V2 provides to MSM may be unsuitable for MSM to find the most effective direction to adjust its weight.
Inspired by this point, we set the backbone of MSM to another simplified Inception network (shown in Figure 5) which has a more similar architecture to IncRes-V2 than ResNet-19. 
Our motivation is that **the gradient of the simplified Inception backbone may be more similar to that of IncRes-V2 than ResNet-19 so that the feedback information from IncRes-V2 is effective to optimize the weight of MSM.**

In Table 2, the comparison between MTA and MTA$\_{Inc}$ shows that MTA can be clearly improved by changing the architecture of MSM from ResNet-19 to the simplified Inception network.
**This experimental result demonstrates our guess and also inspires us to improve MTA by finding more suitable backbone for MSM.**

Thanks for your feedback.
I want to explain the architecture of MSM more detailedly.
Choosing the architecture for MSM does not matter with the target model.
We can know the architecture of the source model in the TRUE BLACK BOX setting.
Given the source model, we can choose a suitable backbone for MSM so that the MSM is easier to be trained to generate adversarial examples to fool the source model, which will improve the training of MSM and further improve the transfer attack performance on the unknown target model.
For instance, when using the IncRes-V2 source model, we‘d better change the architecture of MSM from ResNet-19 to a simplified Inception network. The reason is that the simplified Inception network is more suitable than ResNet-19 to generate the adversarial examples that are more transferable to attack the IncRes-V2 source model, which will make the bi-level training process of MSM easier. By choosing a more suitable architecture, the bi-level training process becomes easier, and the MSM converges more easily, and finally, the inference performance of MSM can be improved.

content.title: Response to Reviewer cXab
content.comment:
Thanks for your timely reply.

Given the label set of the target model, we can prepare source models by training them on the dataset contains the same label set as the target model. Then, according to the architectures of the source models, we can design a backbone for MSM so that bi-level training the MSM on the source models can converge easily. 
There are two ways to ensure the SOTA transfer attack performance of MTA:
1. From all our experiments, we can see that the default backbone ResNet-13 or -19 is suitable for MSM in most cases. But in a few cases, the backbone ResNet-13 or -19 may need to be adjusted according to the source model architectures (e.g., when the source model is IncRes-V2). In these few cases, we can design a new backbone for the MSM so that the performance of MTA can be improved (see the results in Table 2). According to the convergence curve of the MSM, we can judge whether the backbone of MSM is suitable for the source models. In our experiment, we found a phenomenon that the bi-level training process of MSM will be slow to converge or even somewhat unstable if the MSM backbone is unsuitable for the source models. Therefore we can modify the MSM backbone according to the convergence curve of MSM, or we can use Network Architecture Search (NAS) methods to automatically find the most suitable MSM backbone. In conclusion, we can **ensure the SOTA performance of MTA by adjusting the MSM backbone**.
2. We can also **ensure the SOTA performance of MTA by changing the source model architectures**. Table 2 shows that Inception-V3 or -V4 is friendly to be used as the source model for the bi-level training of MSM. Therefore, we can prepare more friendly source models for MTA to ensure the SOTA performance. 

When there exists a domain gap between the training data of the target model and that of the source model, the transfer attack performances of all methods (including baselines) will be possibly damaged. In our opinion, a straightforward way to ensure the SOTA performance of MTA is to use the training dataset that contains more domain variation.

We hope that our response has addressed your concerns, and turns your assessment to the positive side. If you have other comments, we are glad to address them.

display_title: Response to question: clarity how is MTA and IR combine?

content.title: Response to question: clarity how is MTA and IR combine?
content.comment:
Thanks for your remind. We illustrated MTA-IR more detailedly in Section 4.2.2 of the rebuttal revision.
IR generates adversarial examples by directly attacking source models with IR-PGD.  
MTA generates adversarial examples by attacking the meta-surrogate model with PGD in inference.  
The combination MTA-IR generates adversarial examples by attacking the meta-surrogate model with IR-PGD in inference.  
Therefore, we can formulate the adversarial example generation processes of IR, MTA, and MTA-IR as $x_{adv}=IR(source \ model, x, y)$, $x_{adv}=PGD(MSM, x, y)$, and $x_{adv}=IR(MSM, x, y)$, respectively, where $x$ and $y$ are the victim image and the label, respectively.

display_title: Response to question: Can we properly define success rate in experiments?

content.title: Response to question: Can we properly define success rate in experiments?
content.comment:
The formulation of attack success rate is $Rate =\frac{Card(Set_A)}{Card(Set_B)}$.
$Set_A$ is the set containing all clean images that are correctly classified by model $M$. 
$Set_B$ is the set containing all clean images that not only are correctly classified by model $M$ but also the corresponding adversarial images are misclassified by model $M$.
$Card(Set_A)$ denotes the number of elements in $Set_A$.
We have included the definition of success rate in Section A.7 of the revision.

display_title: Response to question: This paper could have been better it experiments have been conducted in the case where the target model's dataset is unknown

content.title: Response to question: This paper could have been better it experiments have been conducted in the case where the target model's dataset is unknown
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable question.
To address your concern, we performed another experiment on Cifar-10.
Cifar-10 contains 10 categories and each category in the training set contains 5000 images.

In this experiment, we split the training set into **two sub-training sets and each sub-training set contains all the 10 categories.
Every category in the first sub-training set contains 2500 images and every category in the second sub-training set contains the remaining 2500 images.**
Therefore, there are no overlapping images between the two sub-training sets, and the two sub-training sets share only the label set.
We use the first sub-training set to train the source models and the meta-surrogate model, and use the second sub-training set to train the target models.
Thus the source models and the meta-surrogate model does not know the training images of the target models.

The source models are ResNet-10, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-14, SeResNet-26, SeResNet-50, MobileNet-V1, MobileNet-V2 with testing accuracies of 86.8%, 86.7%, 87.2%, 84.2%, 85.4%, 87.7%, 80.7%, and 80.9%, respectively.
The target models are MobileNet-V3, ShuffleNet-V1, ShuffleNet-V2, SqueezeNet-A, and SqueezeNet-B with testing accuracies of 73.9%, 81.1%, 72.6%, 82.3%, and 83.0%, respectively.
Then we use the source models and the trained meta-surrogate model to attack the target models.  
The success rates of PGD are 52.6%, 69.2%, 51.3%, 57.8%, and 60.2%;  
The success rates of MI are 74.4%, 87.1%, 71.6%, 80.3%, and 80.9%;  
The success rates of TI are 56.3%, 59.1%, 56.1%, 63.3%, and 62.0%;  
The success rates of DI are 61.2%, 75.0%, 57.9%, 63.2%, and 66.5%;  
The success rates of TI-DIM are 54.1%, 54.3%, 55.0%, 60.1%, and 57.5%;  
The success rates of MTA are **87.9%, 95.1%, 85.6%, 82.7%, and 83.5%.**  
It is clear that when we know the label set but **do not know the training images of the target models, MTA still outperforms the baselines with clear margins.**
This experiment has been included in Section A.3.6 of the revision.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1454 by Reviewer V2aQ

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper further delves deeper into the question of how to improve the transferability of black-box adversarial examples. It optimizes parameters of a meta-surrogate model using a bi-level optimization problem such that the adversarial examples generated from it have maximum transferability to target models.
content.main_review:
*Strengths*

Proposed approach achieves a significantly better transfer rate than all baselines approaches. It also brings the work on bilevel optimization to adversarial example generation, which is an important contribution. 

*Weaknesses*

I believe that the analyses of the proposed attack success can be further improved by accounting a more realistic set of target models . 

First the paper takes a traditional approach and measures the success of black-box attacks predominantly on non-robust networks. Since early work on adversarial attacks, a lot of research has been conducted in making robust training faster for commonly used datasets. Thus it's likely that the targeted model (at least on small datasets) will be robustly trained. True that authors do include some robust models (on both cifar10 and Imagenet), but there is a larger difference between the perturbation used to train the model (3/255) vs budget used to attack the models (16/255). 

As the authors note, black-box attacks are much faster than query based attacks, thus most suitable for attacking large scale systems. However, the paper lacks experiment working with large scale real-world black-box systems, such cloud prediction APIs offered by common machine learning as a service systems. I encourage authors to test transferability of their attacks on these systems. 

I understand that sometimes we have to follow a common setup from previous works to do a fair comparison. However, in doing so we keep inheriting the same biases from earlier works. For example, one might get the wrong idea that black-box attacks are 97% effective (table-1) even on robustly trained models (which is untrue since attack accuracy on cifar-10 at epsilon 8/255 is ~50% [1]). This claim is fundamentally arising from the issue that there is a mismatch between training and test perturbation budgets.

It will be helpful if each table also includes results on white-box attacks. Since black-box attacks are strictly sub-optimal than white-box attacks, this upper bound will help to calibrate the results. 

It is also unclear how the meta-surrogate model is used practically? Is it a pre-trained network, trained using natural/vanilla training? Are the parameters of the MSM optimized individually for every single image (equation 3), which, if true, is a big efficiency drawback. 

1. https://robustbench.github.io

display_title: Response to question: It is also unclear how the meta-surrogate model is used practically?

content.title: Response to question: It is also unclear how the meta-surrogate model is used practically?
content.comment:
Thanks for your question. The meta-surrogate model is not a pre-trained model. It is a trained model that can be directly used for transfer attack without fine-tuning for each victim image and each victim model.
When attacking a victim image and a victim black-box target models in practice, we generate the corresponding adversarial example by directly attacking the meta-surrogate model without any fine-tuning. In other words, the meta-surrogate model is generalizable to be attacked to generate transferable adversarial examples for all testing images. Therefore, there is no fine-tuning computational cost when we use the meta-surrogate model in practice. **Furthermore, as introduced in Section A.8, MTA greatly saves the computational cost in inference, compared with baselines.**
For example, on ImageNet, when using the Res-152, Res-50, and DN-161 source models, the PGD-based baselines (DI, MI, TI, SGM) cost about 124.1 GFLOPs per gradient ascent step per image, and cost about 109.1M parameters. As a comparison, the inference cost of MTA is only 11.3 GFLOPs per gradient ascent step per image and the MTA needs only 6.77M parameters.
Both $T_v$ (the number of gradient ascent steps on each image in inference) of PGD-based baselines and $T_t$ of MTA are set to 10 in our work.
In conclusion, MTA costs less computational budget than baselines in inference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduces "Meta-Surrogate Model" to improve the transferability of adversarial examples, which optimize a Meta-Surrogate Model(MSM) by bi-level optimization procedure, w.r.t generate adversarial examples by MSM first, feed them to other source models(single or multiple), then optimize the weight of MSM to maximize the losses of source models. Then attack the victim model with adversarial examples generated by MSM.
content.main_review:
The method is new to the best of my knowledge, and the paper is easy to follow. My concerns are as follows:

1. It's interesting that when using a single source model, it could also outperform baselines by a large margin (Table 2). The optimization objective of MSM is to maximize cross-entropy loss of the source model. But when it comes to using a single source model, directly backpropagating the gradient through the source model seems a better choice to maximize the CE loss, like the I-FGSM does. Why does MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples? I recommend explaining this phenomenon to make the method more solid. And it would be better to provide success rates of white-box attacks in Table 2.
2. display_title: Response to question: Why does MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples?

content.title: Response to question: Why does MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples?
content.comment:
Thanks for your question.
In our opinion, **directly attacking the source models may not be the best way to generate transferable adversarial examples**. This is because the source models are all normally trained to solve image classification tasks but not to solve the transfer attack task. In other words, the normally trained source models are not the most suitable models to solve transfer attack. In our work, we propose a bi-level training objective to leverage the source models to obtain a **meta-surrogate model, which is optimized for generating transferable attacks instead of for standard image classification tasks. This bi-level-training objective forces the meta-surrogate model to concentrate on the transfer attack task but not the image classification task**. The effectiveness of MTA mainly comes from the bi-level training objective and can work well with different number of source models. Even with only one source model, the meta-surrogate model can also be bi-level trained for the transfer attack task. Therefore we can observe good results even under a single source model.

Besides, Figure.7 also shows that when given a single source model (ResNet-152), the generated noise map differs between different methods. 
Figure.7 demonstrates that the **noise map generated by attacking the meta-surrogate model differs greatly from the noise map generated by attacking the source model**.
**Together with the experiments shown in Table 2, we can prove our opinion that directly attacking the source models may is not the best way to generate transferable adversarial examples.
There do exist better surrogate model than the source models to address transfer attack, and the proposed MTA do find such a meta-surrogate model for better transfer attack results.**
Overall, the reason for the question of why does MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples is clear.
Benefits from the proposed MTA framework, we obtain a more suitable surrogate model (MSM) than source models to solve transfer attack.
By attacking the MSM, we can obtain more transferable adversarial examples.

content.title: More Response to question: Why does MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples?
content.comment: The ***key reason*** why MSM could provide more transferable adversarial examples is that ***MSM is trained for transfer attack while the source models are trained for image classification (see Eq.3). In other words, Eq.3 forces MSM to focus on improving the transferability of the adversarial examples generated on it but not classifying images, while all the source models focus on classifying images but not transfer attack. Therefore generating adversarial examples by attacking MSM can produce better transfer attack results than by directly attacking the source models.***

content.title: Response to question: Success rates of white-box attacks in Table 2?
content.comment: For the white-box attacks (the target model is the source model itself) in Table 2, we directly use PGD to attack the source model but not to attack the MSM. Therefore, the white-box attack performances in Table 2 are equal to those of the standard PGD. For instance, the white-box attack success rates on Inc-V3, Inc-V4, IncRes-V2, and Res-152 are 99.9%, 99.9%, 98.0%, and 99.1%, respectively. We will include all the white-box attack results in our next version.
